questions.stem: A patient develops high-volume dilute urine after a head injury. Which mechanism best fits central diabetes insipidus?
questions.rationale: Head injury can disrupt ADH release. Less ADH reduces renal water reabsorption.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes insipidus has normal ADH secretion. What defect best explains the persistent polyuria?
questions.rationale: Nephrogenic DI results when the kidneys respond inadequately to ADH.

questions.stem: A patient with SIADH has low serum osmolality. Which urine finding best supports ongoing ADH activity?
questions.rationale: ADH continues to promote water reabsorption, leaving urine relatively concentrated.

options.text: Urine concentration that falls appropriately as serum dilutes
High urine output with falling serum sodium
Very dilute urine with high output

questions.stem: A patient with untreated DI cannot replace urinary water losses. Which serum pattern is expected?
questions.rationale: Water loss in excess of replacement concentrates serum sodium and raises osmolality.

options.text: Falling sodium and rising osmolality from water retention
Stable sodium with progressively diluted serum

questions.stem: What directly explains hyponatremia in SIADH?
questions.rationale: Excess ADH promotes water retention, diluting serum sodium.

options.text: The kidneys fail to filter any sodium
Low ADH causes loss of free water

questions.stem: A client with SIADH becomes confused as sodium falls. Which change best accounts for the symptom?
questions.rationale: Hypotonic hyponatremia can cause brain cell swelling and neurologic symptoms.

options.text: Hypotonic plasma promotes water movement into brain cells
Concentrated plasma draws water out of brain cells
Increased blood glucose causes osmotic diuresis
Elevated urine osmolality directly raises brain sodium

questions.stem: Select exactly two findings that favor DI in a client who cannot keep up with urinary losses.
questions.rationale: With inadequate ADH action, the kidneys excrete large volumes of dilute urine.

questions.stem: A patient with DI becomes tachycardic and dizzy when standing. What change best explains this trend?
questions.rationale: Urinary water loss can reduce circulating volume, causing compensatory tachycardia and orthostatic symptoms.

options.text: Loss of water reduces circulating volume

questions.stem: Match each ADH-related finding to its profile.
questions.rationale: Serum and urine osmolality change in opposite directions in both disorders.

targets.text: High when water losses exceed intake

questions.stem: The nurse reviews these provider orders for suspected SIADH. Which statements explain why the tests are paired? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: The serum tests assess dilution and the urine test assesses whether the kidney is appropriately excreting dilute urine.

exhibit.title: Provider orders
exhibit.text: Obtain serum sodium and serum osmolality. Obtain urine osmolality.

options.text: Urine testing can show urine that remains concentrated despite dilute serum.
Urine osmolality directly measures serum sodium.
Serum sodium alone distinguishes central from nephrogenic DI.
Serum testing can identify dilutional hyponatremia.

questions.stem: A patient develops proximal muscle weakness and broad purple striae after long-term glucocorticoid use. What hormonal effect best accounts for the pattern?
questions.rationale: Sustained glucocorticoid exposure can cause muscle wasting and skin fragility.

questions.stem: A client with Cushing syndrome develops higher fasting glucose. Which hormone effect contributes?
questions.rationale: Glucocorticoid excess raises glucose through increased hepatic production and insulin resistance.

options.text: Cortisol increases glucose availability and opposes insulin action
Cortisol increases insulin sensitivity and reduces glucose production
Aldosterone directly clears glucose from the blood

questions.stem: Which paired complication is consistent with prolonged cortisol excess?
questions.rationale: Chronic glucocorticoid excess promotes protein breakdown and loss of bone mass.

options.text: Muscle hypertrophy and increased bone density

questions.stem: Why should signs of infection be assessed carefully in a patient with glucocorticoid excess?
questions.rationale: Immune suppression increases susceptibility to infection and can blunt inflammatory signs.

options.text: Glucocorticoid excess blocks exposure to pathogens
Glucocorticoids suppress immune and inflammatory responses
Glucocorticoids directly increase antibody production against all organisms

questions.stem: A client with primary adrenal insufficiency has sodium 128 mEq/L and potassium 5.8 mEq/L. Which loss explains this pairing?
questions.rationale: Aldosterone deficiency reduces renal sodium retention and potassium excretion.

questions.stem: Which finding helps distinguish primary adrenal insufficiency from isolated secondary cortisol deficiency?
questions.rationale: Loss of adrenal cortisol feedback can raise ACTH in primary disease, contributing to hyperpigmentation.

questions.stem: Why can a serious infection precipitate an adrenal crisis in a person with Addison disease?
questions.rationale: Acute illness increases cortisol requirements. Insufficient reserve can trigger crisis.

options.text: The adrenal cortex cannot meet the increased cortisol demand of stress
Infection temporarily restores adrenal hormone production
Stress removes the need for cortisol
Infection leads to a sustained excess of adrenal cortisol

questions.stem: Which two findings in a client with known Addison disease during acute illness are most concerning for adrenal crisis? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Severe hypotension and hypoglycemia fit acute adrenal hormone deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient with Cushing syndrome develops easy bruising after minor contact. Which tissue change explains this?
questions.rationale: Glucocorticoid excess thins skin and weakens connective tissues, making bruising easier.

options.text: Glucocorticoid excess causes skin and connective tissue fragility
Cortisol deficiency strengthens skin and capillaries
Increased collagen synthesis makes the skin thick and elastic

questions.stem: Which cause specifically defines Cushing disease within the broader category of Cushing syndrome?
questions.rationale: Cushing disease refers specifically to pituitary ACTH-driven cortisol excess.

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex

questions.stem: A patient eats more than usual but loses weight and feels overheated. Which process explains both findings?
questions.rationale: Thyroid hormone excess increases energy expenditure and heat production.

options.text: Excess thyroid hormone increases metabolic rate
Low thyroid hormone increases basal energy use

questions.stem: Which pulse finding fits untreated hypothyroidism with fatigue and cold intolerance?
questions.rationale: Reduced thyroid activity can slow the heart rate.

options.text: A resting rate that rises from excess thyroid hormone
A rapid irregular pulse with severe heat intolerance

questions.stem: Why can hypothyroidism contribute to constipation?
questions.rationale: Slower intestinal transit favors constipation.

options.text: Reduced thyroid activity slows GI motility
Excess thyroid activity slows gastric and colonic transit
Increased motility leaves stool in the colon longer
Low ADH reduces intestinal contractions directly

questions.stem: Which finding in an otherwise hyperthyroid client is particularly associated with Graves disease?
questions.rationale: Graves disease can cause orbitopathy with exophthalmos.

options.text: Periorbital puffiness with a thick tongue

questions.stem: Which finding fits myxedema in severe hypothyroidism?
questions.rationale: Myxedema can produce facial and periorbital puffiness and tongue thickening.

questions.stem: Which two findings are consistent with excess thyroid hormone? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Tremor and tachycardia fit thyroid hormone excess. The remaining findings favor hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A client with a goiter asks if that alone means the thyroid is overactive. Which response is accurate?
questions.rationale: Goiter describes thyroid enlargement. Hormone measurements help determine thyroid function.

options.text: Goiter establishes hypothyroidism without hormone testing
Goiter establishes that thyroid hormone levels are normal
Goiter can occur with either hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism
Goiter establishes hyperthyroidism without hormone testing

questions.stem: A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism develops extreme tachycardia, fever and agitation. Which complication fits?
questions.rationale: An acute escalation of hyperthyroid manifestations raises concern for thyroid storm.

questions.stem: A client with long-standing hypothyroidism becomes difficult to arouse and hypothermic. Which complication fits?
questions.rationale: Severe decompensated hypothyroidism can cause hypothermia and depressed mental status.

questions.stem: Match each term to its associated finding or disorder.
questions.rationale: Graves and Hashimoto are autoimmune disorders with different hormone effects. Their severe complications reflect excess and deficiency respectively.

questions.stem: Which process causes the severe insulin deficiency of type 1 diabetes?
questions.rationale: Beta cell destruction removes the body's main source of insulin.

options.text: Increased sensitivity of skeletal muscle to insulin
Increased release of insulin after meals

questions.stem: Why can a patient with early type 2 diabetes have hyperglycemia while still producing insulin?
questions.rationale: Insulin resistance limits glucose uptake and the suppression of hepatic glucose output.

options.text: All pancreatic beta cells have already been destroyed
Insulin production reliably exceeds the body's needs
Target tissues respond inadequately to insulin
Excess ADH prevents glucose entry into cells

questions.stem: Why may a client with type 2 diabetes require insulin later in the course of the disease?
questions.rationale: Progressive beta cell dysfunction can make endogenous insulin insufficient.

options.text: Insulin treatment is used only when all beta cells are destroyed
The disease stops affecting glucose regulation over time
Beta cell output can decline until it no longer compensates for insulin resistance
Insulin resistance always resolves as the disease progresses

questions.stem: A client with hyperglycemia develops polyuria. Which mechanism explains the increase in urine volume?
questions.rationale: Filtered glucose that remains in the tubule retains water and increases urine output.

options.text: Glucose in the filtrate increases water reabsorption directly
Serum glucose blocks all renal filtration
Insulin resistance prevents glucose from entering the filtrate
Glucose in the filtrate retains water and promotes osmotic diuresis

questions.stem: Why does severe insulin deficiency promote ketone formation?
questions.rationale: When insulin is severely deficient, lipolysis supplies fatty acids for ketogenesis.

options.text: Increased fat breakdown supplies substrate for hepatic ketone production
Increased insulin stimulates fat storage and ketone production
Glucose in urine is converted to ketones in the bladder
ADH stimulates direct conversion of glucose to ketones

questions.stem: A client with diabetes has pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L and PaCO₂ 26 mm Hg. Reference ranges are pH 7.35–7.45, bicarbonate 22–26 mEq/L and PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg. Which pattern fits?
questions.rationale: Low pH and bicarbonate identify metabolic acidosis. Low PaCO₂ reflects compensatory ventilation.

questions.stem: Why does a client in DKA develop deep, rapid breathing?
questions.rationale: Kussmaul respirations increase carbon dioxide elimination as compensation for metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Deep breathing directly increases serum bicarbonate production
Increased ventilation lowers carbon dioxide to compensate for metabolic acidosis
Increased ventilation raises carbon dioxide to correct the acidosis
Ketones stop the respiratory response to low pH

questions.stem: An older client with type 2 diabetes has glucose 728 mg/dL, high serum osmolality and minimal ketones. Which condition best fits?
questions.rationale: Marked hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with minimal ketosis fit HHS.

questions.stem: Select exactly two findings that favor DKA over HHS.
questions.rationale: Significant ketonemia and the resulting acidosis distinguish DKA. Both states can cause glucosuria and dehydration.

questions.stem: Put the events in order from severe insulin deficiency to the respiratory response in DKA.
questions.rationale: Severe insulin deficiency promotes lipolysis and ketogenesis. The resulting metabolic acidosis triggers compensatory ventilation.

options.text: Ketone acids accumulate and bicarbonate falls
Deep rapid breathing compensates for acidosis
Fat breakdown supplies fatty acids to the liver
